corrections.from: Radiocarbon birth dating reads a cell population's genomic DNA as one date mark:
corrections.finding: Six findings, one fixed item. (1) The field's words are carried bare in the item's own voice: "genomic DNA is not exchanged after a cell has gone through its last division" and "the 14C level in DNA serves as a date mark for when a cell was born" stand unmarked, so a negation (not exchanged) and a released word (when) sit at the file's own voice; a field's word holds whole only in quotation (Natural Naming 2.7, 2.4 at *when*), and the gathering-value's own idiom is "a field's own words" with straight quotes. Re-said with both quotations marked as the field's, the third as the slice gives it, a field's account. (2) "The two papers' texts name no strand made before the last division" is not a measure the source did not read: the source read both texts and the observing returned nothing. Said so it is a publishing reference (the two papers) and a negation with a doer (texts naming); its positive, the texts' own, is that the genomic DNA is one date mark at its last division, which the field's words hold, and with the positive in the lead the denial is scaffolding and goes (Natural Explaining 3.3). (3) The explaining is mislabelled "A re-saying beside the sentence": it re-says no living-file sentence, it explains the field's date mark; the file's idiom is "An explaining beside it". Within it "so a chain's carbon is" is a forcing (so at a reason, Natural Naming 2.4; therefore, Natural Explaining 3.6), re-said by a colon; and "formed at it from carbon ingested then" has an -ed and a then over a momentarying, re-said as forms, of carbon atoms, at that fork. (4) Part of the source's explaining is dropped: "prior-existing with the cell" and "now-existing with it", the two moments' seating at the opening's prior-existing and now-existing, and "a strand retained is a strand whose carbon is older than its cell", the nonrandom case's own claim; all three restored. (5) The explaining's *chain* takes two senses: a strand at "one chain of each pair" and the double chain at "a chain's carbon is one half from the last fork" (a strand's carbon atoms are from one fork; the halves, quarters and eighths are a pair's, both strands, which is what a population measuring of genomic DNA reads). The halves are said of a pair, one sense per word (Natural Naming 2.5), the numbers unchanged: one half, one quarter, one eighth, about one fork interval, and the whole line of forks under nonrandom segregation, all the explaining's own and none the field's. The anticipated observing stays binary, is or is not, in the source's word fork rather than the item's swap to division, so one word runs through the item. Carbon is said as carbon atoms, the file's own word at 4.7. (6) "Each new molecule has one original strand and one fresh." is held: it is the sentence the item meets, and its ground, density labelling, is held at gathering-value 4.7 "Escherichia coli grown for several generations on heavy nitrogen (15N) ... every daughter double helix is of one parent strand and one strand newly made."; it leaves the item. The slice's purine-ring and chromatid-segregation lines are likewise held, at 4.6 "Each purine ring made anew in a cell takes one carbon atom, C6, from bicarbonate ..." and 4.7 "Blood-forming stem cells of mice given bromodeoxyuridine ... about 85 percent of divisions ...", and the item's nonrandom case carries no number that parts from them. The value itself, a date mark one number read from two moments, older than its last fork by about one fork interval under random segregation and by the whole line under strand retention, with its binary observing, is held at no living file and no gathering-value line, and 4.7 is its section.

fixed.section: 4.7 DNA replication and repair — the self copying itself, and the protection of the copying
fixed.sentence: Two strands of double helix separate, and each serves as template for a new complementary strand, each new molecule with one original strand and one fresh — a self recursioning to two, each bringing form forward.
fixed.text: A field's radiocarbon birth dating has a cell population's genomic DNA as one date mark at its last division, in a field's own words "genomic DNA, which is not exchanged after a cell has gone through its last division" and "the 14C level in DNA serves as a date mark for when a cell was born", and the method gives an average age for a cell population. An explaining beside it: at a cell's last fork one chain of each pair is the same thing it was before that fork, prior-existing with the cell, and the other forms at that fork of carbon atoms the cell ingests at it, now-existing with the cell: one pair, two moments, prior-existing across from now-existing, and a field's date mark is one number read from two. With random chromatid segregation the pair at the fork before is itself half from the fork before that: a pair's carbon atoms are one half from the last fork, one quarter from the one before and one eighth from the one before that, and a population's one number stands older than its last fork by about one fork interval; with nonrandom segregation the older half is older by the whole line of forks, and a strand retained is a strand whose carbon atoms are older than its cell. An anticipated observing, binary: in a tissue with a measured fork interval a field's radiocarbon birth date is or is not older than the last fork's date by that interval, and in a stem cell with a retained strand, older by more.
